text: Jaime Royal "Robbie" Robertson OC (July 5, 1943 – August 9, 2023) was a Canadian musician, composer, and producer. He was the lead guitarist for Bob Dylan's backing band and the guitarist and primary songwriter of The Band from its formation until his departure in 1976. In his later solo career, he released six albums. Robertson's work with The Band was instrumental in creating the Americana music genre. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Canadian Music Hall of Fame as a member of The Band, and also into Canada's Walk of Fame, both with The Band and individually. He is ranked 59th in Rolling Stone magazine's 2011 list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time. He co-wrote "The Weight" and "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down" with The Band and had a solo hit with "Somewhere Down the Crazy River." He was inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame and received a Lifetime Achievement Award from the National Academy of Songwriters. Robertson collaborated on film and television soundtracks, primarily with director Martin Scorsese. His soundtrack work began with The Band's farewell rockumentary film The Last Waltz (1978) and included dramatic films such as Raging Bull (1980), The King of Comedy (1983), The Color of Money (1986), The Irishman (2019), and Killers of the Flower Moon (2023), the latter dedicated to his memory and earning him a posthumous Academy Award nomination for Best Original Score. Born on July 5, 1943, Robertson's mother, Rosemarie Dolly Chrysler, was born on February 6, 1922. Chrysler was Cayuga and Mohawk, raised on the Six Nations of the Grand River reserve southwest of Toronto near Hamilton, and later lived with an aunt in Toronto's Cabbagetown neighbourhood, working at the Coro jewellery plating factory, where she met James Patrick Robertson and married him in 1942. James and Rosemarie Robertson continued working at the Coro factory and lived in several Toronto neighbourhoods while Robbie was a child. An only child, Robertson often visited the Six Nations reserve with his mother, where he was taught guitar by his older cousin Herb Myke. He became a fan of rock and roll and rhythm and blues through radio, listening to disc jockey George "Hound Dog" Lorenz on WKBW from Buffalo, New York, and John R.'s all-night blues show on WLAC, a clear-channel station in Nashville, Tennessee. At age 12, his mother told him his biological father was Alexander David Klegerman, a Jewish-American gambler with whom she had been involved before marrying James Robertson; Klegerman died in a hit-and-run accident on the Queen Elizabeth Way before Robbie was born. Robertson's mother arranged for him to meet his paternal uncles, Morris (Morrie) and Nathan (Natie) Klegerman, who "quickly pulled me into their world and went out of their way to make me feel like family." At 14, he worked two brief summer jobs in the travelling carnival circuit, first in a Toronto suburb and later as an assistant at a freak show during the Canadian National Exhibition. He later drew from this experience for the song "Life is a Carnival" (with The Band) and the movie Carny (1980), which he both produced and starred in. His first band was Little Caesar and the Consuls, formed in 1956 by Bruce Morshead and Gene MacLellan, which he joined for almost a year. In 1957, he formed Robbie and the Rhythm Chords with Pete "Thumper" Traynor, later changing the name to Robbie and the Robots after watching Forbidden Planet and liking its character Robby the Robot. Traynor customized Robertson's guitar with antennae and wires. The group later became The Suedes with pianist Scott Cushnie. At a show on October 5, 1959, at CHUM Radio's Hif Fi Club on Toronto's Merton Street, Ronnie Hawkins first became aware of them and was impressed enough to join them for a few numbers. Robertson began shadowing Hawkins after the Suedes opened for him at Dixie Arena. One afternoon, he overheard Hawkins say he needed new songs for a studio session, so he stayed up all night and wrote "Someone Like You" and "Hey Boba Lu," which he played for Hawkins the next day. Hawkins recorded both for his album Mr Dynamo (1959) and brought Robertson to the Brill Building in New York to help choose songs. Hawkins hired pianist Scott Cushnie away from The Suedes and took him on tour in Arkansas. When the Hawks' bass player left, Cushnie recommended hiring Robertson to replace him on bass. Hawkins invited Robertson to Arkansas and then flew to the UK to perform there. Left in Arkansas, Robertson spent his living allowance on records and practiced daily. Upon returning, Hawkins hired him to play bass. Cushnie left the band a few months later. Robertson soon switched from bass to lead guitar for the Hawks, developing into a guitar virtuoso. Roy Buchanan, a few years older than Robertson, briefly joined the Hawks and influenced Robertson's guitar style through his volume speed dial use, string bending, rapid sweep picking, and passion for bending past root and fifth notes. Drummer/singer Levon Helm was already a member of the Hawks and soon became close friends with Robertson. The Hawks continued touring the U.S. and Canada, adding Rick Danko, Richard Manuel, and Garth Hudson in 1961, forming the lineup that later became The Band. They toured with Hawkins throughout 1962 and into 1963 and also hired saxophonists Jerry Penfound and Bruce Bruno. The Hawks recorded sessions for Roulette Records from 1961 to 1963, producing three singles: "Come Love" b/w "I Feel Good" (Roulette 4400, 1961); "Who Do You Love" b/w "Bo Diddley" (Roulette 4483, 1963); and "There's A Screw Loose" b/w "High Blood Pressure" (Roulette 4502, 1963). In early 1964, the group left Ronnie Hawkins and began seeking new direction, losing interest in rockabilly and favoring blues and soul. They approached agent Harold Kudlets, who agreed to represent them and booked them in the same circuits as before. Initially dubbed The Levon Helm Sextet, the group included all future members of The Band, plus Jerry Penfound and Bob Bruno. After Bruno left in May 1964, the group changed their name to Levon and the Hawks. Penfound stayed until 1965. Kudlets kept them busy performing throughout 1964 and 1965, booking two lengthy summer engagements at Tony Mart's in Somers Point, New Jersey, playing six nights a week alongside Conway Twitty. In 1964, the group befriended blues artist John P. Hammond in Toronto. Later that year, they worked on Hammond's album So Many Roads (released in 1965), with Robertson playing guitar and being billed as "Jaime R. Robertson" in the credits. In March 1965, under the name the Canadian Squires, they released the single "Uh Uh Uh" b/w "Leave Me Alone," both songs written by Robertson, recorded in New York, and released on Apex Records in the U.S. and Ware Records in Canada. In 1965, as Levon and the Hawks, they recorded an afternoon session for Atco Records, yielding two singles: "The Stones I Throw" b/w "He Don't Love You" (Atco 6383) and "Go, Go, Liza Jane" b/w "He Don't Love You" (Atco 6625), all written by Robertson. In August 1965, Robertson received a call from Albert Grossman Management requesting a meeting with Bob Dylan. The group had been recommended to both Grossman and Dylan by Mary Martin, a Toronto-born employee of Grossman and a friend of the band, and Dylan was also aware of them through John Hammond, whose album So Many Roads the group had performed on. Robertson agreed to meet with Dylan, initially refusing to join as guitarist but agreeing to play two shows: one at the Forest Hills Tennis Stadium on August 28 and one at the Hollywood Bowl on September 3, suggesting Levon Helm play drums. The first show received a hostile response, while the second was slightly more favorable. Dylan flew to Toronto and rehearsed with Levon and the Hawks from September 15 to 17, after which he hired the full band for his upcoming tour, making Robertson his guitarist during his "legendary electric period." Dylan and the Hawks toured the U.S. from October to December 1965, with each show featuring two sets: an acoustic set with Dylan alone and an electric set with the Hawks. The tours were met with hostility from fans who viewed Dylan's shift to rock as a betrayal. Helm left after the November 28 performance in Washington, D.C. On November 30, 1965, Dylan recorded a studio session with the Hawks, producing the non-LP single "Can You Please Crawl Out Your Window?" Dylan completed the Blonde on Blonde album in Nashville in mid-February 1966, with Robertson participating in a session on February 14. Dylan and the Hawks played more dates in the continental U.S. from February to March 1966, followed by tours in Hawaii, Australia, Europe, and the UK and Ireland from April 9 to May 27. The Australian and European legs received particularly harsh reactions from disgruntled folk fans. The May 17 Manchester Free Trade Hall show is best known for an audience member yelling "Judas!" at Dylan, becoming a frequently-bootlegged live recording later officially released as The Bootleg Series Vol. 4: Bob Dylan Live 1966, The "Royal Albert Hall" Concert. On July 29, 1966, Dylan suffered a neck injury in a motorcycle accident and retreated to a quiet life in upstate New York. Some Hawks members lived at the Chelsea Hotel in New York and were kept on a weekly retainer by Dylan's management. In February 1967, Dylan invited the Hawks to Woodstock, New York to work on music. Robertson had met a French-Canadian woman during a stop on Dylan's 1966 world tour and moved into a house in the Woodstock area. The remaining three members of the Hawks rented a house near West Saugerties, New York, later known as "Big Pink" due to its pink exterior. Dylan and the Hawks worked daily at Big Pink to rehearse and generate song ideas, many of which were recorded in the basement studio between late spring and autumn of 1967. Previous Hawks member Levon Helm returned to the group in August 1967. By this time, Robertson's guitar style had evolved to be more supportive of the songs and less focused on speed and virtuosity. In 1968, Rolling Stone co-founder Jann Wenner highlighted these sessions in an article titled "Dylan's Basement Tape Should Be Released." In 1969, a bootleg album with a plain white cover, compiled by two incognito music industry insiders, featured seven tracks from these sessions and became known as The Great White Wonder. It gained popularity in independent record stores and on radio, becoming a runaway success and helping to launch the bootleg recording industry. In 1975, Robertson produced an official compilation, The Basement Tapes, which included selected tracks from the sessions. An exhaustive collection of all 138 extant recordings was released in 2014 as The Bootleg Series Vol. 11: The Basement Tapes Complete. In late 1967, Dylan left to record John Wesley Harding (1967). After recording the basic tracks, Dylan asked Robertson and Garth Hudson to play on the album to fill out the sound, but Robertson liked the starkness and recommended leaving the tracks as they were. Dylan worked with the Hawks again for two Woody Guthrie memorial concerts at Carnegie Hall in January 1968, with three performances later released on the LP A Tribute to Woody Guthrie, Vol. 1 (1972). During the "Basement Tapes" period, the group developed their own sound. Grossman went to Los Angeles to shop the group to a major label, securing a contract with Capitol Records. The group went to New York to begin recording with music producer John Simon, and Capitol brought them to Los Angeles.

In late 1967, Dylan left to record John Wesley Harding (1967), after which he asked Robertson and Garth Hudson if they would play on the album to complete the sound; Robertson appreciated the raw quality and advised leaving the tracks as is. Dylan later worked with the Hawks again during two Woody Guthrie memorial concerts at Carnegie Hall in January 1968, with three of these performances released as A Tribute to Woody Guthrie, Vol. 1 (1972). Over the "Basement Tapes" period, the group developed their own sound; Grossman moved to Los Angeles to secure a contract with Capitol Records, and the group began recording with producer John Simon in New York before finishing in Los Angeles. The resulting album, Music from Big Pink, was released in August 1968 and marked the debut studio album of the group, which called itself The Band. Robertson was the principal songwriter and lead guitarist, writing four songs for Music from Big Pink—“The Weight,” “Chest Fever,” “Caledonia Mission,” and “To Kingdom Come”—credited as “J.R. Robertson,” and sang lead on “To Kingdom Come”; he did not sing on another public Band song until “Knockin’ Lost John” on 1977’s Islands. “The Weight” was influenced by Luis Buñuel’s films, particularly Nazarín (1959) and Viridiana (1961), reflecting the theme of sainthood being unattainable, and the mention of “Nazareth” referenced the C. F. Martin & Company guitar manufacturer in Nazareth, Pennsylvania, where Robertson saw the word in his guitar. Although “The Weight” reached No. 21 on the British radio charts and initially stalled at No. 63 on the American charts, it became the Band’s best-known song, covered by many artists and appearing in numerous films and documentaries. The Band began performing regularly in spring 1969, with their first live dates at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco, and notable performances at the 1969 Woodstock Festival and the UK Isle of Wight Festival with Bob Dylan in August. Their self-titled second album, released in September 1969, was a critical and commercial success, peaking at No. 9 on the U.S. pop charts and staying in the Top 40 for 24 weeks; Robertson wrote or co-wrote every song, and the album is recognized as a foundational work in the Americana music genre and was included in the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry in 2009. “The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down,” written by Robertson over eight months, tells of the suffering of Virgil Caine, a poor white Southerner during the final days of the American Civil War; Robertson developed the concept with help from Helm, a native of Arkansas, and the song was first released as the B side of “Up on Cripple Creek,” which reached No. 3 in 1971, helping popularize it. The song was ranked number 245 on Rolling Stone’s 2004 list of the 500 greatest songs of all time, named the forty-second best song of the 1960s by Pitchfork, and included in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame’s “500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll” and Time magazine’s All-Time 100. On November 2, 1969, the Band appeared on the Ed Sullivan Show, one of only two television appearances they made; on January 12, 1970, they were featured on the cover of Time magazine. Planning to record a live album at The Woodstock Playhouse, the city council denied the request, so they recorded without an audience; Robertson handled most songwriting duties and brought in Todd Rundgren to engineer the sessions, which took two weeks and resulted in Stage Fright, the Band’s highest-charting album, peaking at No. 5 and staying in the Top 40 for 14 weeks. Their next album, Cahoots, recorded at Albert Grossman’s Bearsville Studios and released in October 1971, received mixed reviews, peaked at No. 24, and remained in the Top 40 for five weeks; it included a cover of Bob Dylan’s “When I Paint My Masterpiece,” which came about when Dylan played an unfinished version to Robertson, leading to the Band recording it; the album also featured “Life Is a Carnival.” The Band toured throughout 1970–1971, and a live album from shows at the Academy of Music in New York City from December 28–31, 1971, was released in 1972 as Rock of Ages, which peaked at No. 6 and stayed in the Top 40 for 14 weeks. After the Academy of Music shows, the Band stopped touring and returned to the stage on July 28, 1973, performing at the Summer Jam at Watkins Glen alongside the Allman Brothers Band and the Grateful Dead; the performance was released as Live at Watkins Glen in 1995 and drew over 600,000 attendees, setting a record for “Pop Festival Attendance” in the Guinness Book of World Records (first published in 1976). In October 1973, the Band released Moondog Matinee, which peaked at No. 28; during its recording, Robertson began working on an unfinished project called Works. One lyric from Works, “Lay a flower in the snow,” was used in Robertson’s song “Fallen Angel” on his 1987 solo album. Bill Graham ran a full-page advertisement in The New York Times to promote the 1974 tour with Bob Dylan and received between five and six million ticket requests for 650,000 seats; tickets were sold via lottery, and Dylan and the Band earned $2 million. While preparing for the tour, the Band recorded Planet Waves (1974) with Dylan at Village Recorder in West Los Angeles from November 2–14, 1973; the album was released on February 9, 1974, reached No. 1 on the Billboard charts for four weeks, and spent 12 weeks in the Top 40; it was Bob Dylan’s first No. 1 album and the only studio album recorded together with the Band. The 1974 tour began on January 3 in Chicago and ended on February 14 at The Forum in Inglewood, California; the final three shows were compiled into Before the Flood, released on July 20, 1974, credited to “Bob Dylan/The Band,” debuted at No. 3, and spent ten weeks in the Top 40. After the tour, manager Elliot Roberts booked the Band with Crosby, Stills, Nash, and Young, who performed together at Wembley Stadium in London on September 4 with Jesse Colin Young and Joni Mitchell. After moving to Malibu in 1973, Robertson and the Band leased a ranch near Zuma Beach called “Shangri-La”; the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes, credited to Bob Dylan and the Band, was the first album produced at the new studio, featuring selected tapes from the 1967 sessions and demos for Music from Big Pink, with Robertson cleaning up the tracks and releasing it in July 1975. One of the most notable tracks on Northern Lights – Southern Cross (1975), released on November 1, is “Acadian Driftwood,” the Band’s first song with Canadian subject matter, inspired by the 1971 documentary Acadia, Acadia (L'Acadie, L'Acadie?!?) seen by Robertson in Montreal; the album received positive reviews and reached No. 26 on the Billboard charts, staying in the Top 40 for five weeks. The Band began touring again in June 1976, performing through the summer, but Richard Manuel suffered a neck injury in a boating accident, canceling ten dates. Robertson suggested the group cease touring, agreeing to a “grand finale” show, parting ways to pursue individual projects, and then regrouping; Helm later claimed Robertson forced the breakup, citing concerns about heroin use by Danko, Helm, and Manuel as reasons for Robertson’s departure. On November 25, 1976, the Band performed at the Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving, with ticket prices of $25 and a Thanksgiving dinner served; the event, called The Last Waltz, included musical guests and was filmed by director Martin Scorsese, with a 200-page script developed by Robertson and Scorsese. Warner Bros. Records offered to fund the film in exchange for the right to release the music, and the Band recorded Islands for Capitol between rehearsals, with Robertson writing or co-writing eight of the ten tracks; “Knockin’ Lost John” featured Robertson on vocals, the first since “To Kingdom Come,” and “Christmas Must Be Tonight” was inspired by the birth of Robertson’s son, Sebastian, in July 1974. Approximately 5,000 people attended The Last Waltz; after the concert, Scorsese had 400 reels of raw footage. The Last Waltz album, released on April 7, 1978, as a 3-LP set, featured live performances on the first five sides and studio recordings on the last, including Out of the Blue, which became the third and final Band song with Robertson on lead vocals; it peaked at No. 16 and stayed in the Top 40 for 8 weeks. The film premiered in theaters on April 26, 1978, and received positive reviews from both rock and film critics; Robertson and Scorsese promoted it across America and Europe. Over time, The Last Waltz has been recognized as a pioneering rockumentary, influencing films like Talking Heads’ Stop Making Sense (1984) and U2’s Rattle and Hum (1988); Roger Ebert offered a mixed review, noting the musicians seemed to have bad memories, Scorsese focused on close-ups and ignored the audience, and the film was made during a difficult period in Scorsese’s life. Robertson left the Band in 1976 but performed with them one final time on March 1, 1978, at the Roxy in Los Angeles. Robertson is credited as writer or co-writer of most of The Band’s songs and has received the majority of the songwriting royalties, leading to disputes, especially with Helm, who in his 1993 autobiography, This Wheel’s on Fire, argued that the songs were developed collaboratively and that the credits were invalid; Danko agreed, stating, “I think Levon.”

The Last Waltz was made during a difficult period in Martin Scorsese's life, coinciding with his work on New York, New York, and features mostly closeups and medium shots of performances, ignoring the audience; it does not portray serene or nostalgic scenes of friends enjoying each other's company. Robertson left The Band in 1976 but performed with them one final time on March 1, 1978 at the Roxy in Los Angeles. He is credited as writer or co-writer of most of The Band's songs and thus received the majority of the songwriting royalties, leading to disputes, especially with Helm, who argued in his 1993 autobiography This Wheel's on Fire that the songs were collaboratively developed by all members; Danko agreed, stating that the Band stopped being a true group when Robbie and Albert Grossman took themselves too seriously. Robertson denied Helm wrote any songs attributed to him. He produced and played guitar on Jesse Winchester's 1970 self-titled debut album on Ampex Records, co-crediting "Snow" to himself. He played guitar on Ringo Starr's 1973 album Ringo on the track "Sunshine Life For Me (Sail Away Raymond)" with four-fifths of The Band and contributed a guitar solo to "Snookeroo" on Starr's 1974 album Goodnight Vienna. In 1974, he played guitar on Joni Mitchell's "Raised on Robbery" from Court and Spark and on Carly Simon's version of "Mockingbird" with James Taylor. In 1975, he produced and played guitar on Hirth Martinez's debut album Hirth From Earth, which Bob Dylan had recommended to him; he also played guitar on Martinez's follow-up album Big Bright Street (1977). That same year, Eric Clapton recorded No Reason to Cry at The Band's Shangri-La Studios with members of The Band, with Robertson playing lead guitar on "Sign Language." In the mid-1970s, Robertson collaborated with Neil Diamond on a concept album about a Tin Pan Alley songwriter, Beautiful Noise, recorded at Shangri-La Studios in early 1976; it reached No. 6 on the Billboard charts and stayed in the Top 40 for sixteen weeks. Robertson produced the album, co-wrote "Dry Your Eyes" with Diamond (which he later performed at The Last Waltz), and played guitar on "Dry Your Eyes," "Lady-Oh," and "Jungletime." He also produced Diamond's live double album Love at the Greek (1977), recorded in 1976 at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles, which reached No. 8 on the Billboard charts and stayed in the Top 40 for nine weeks. In 1977, he played guitar on "Java Blues" for Rick Danko's self-titled debut and on "Sing, Sing, Sing" for Levon Helm & the RCO All-Stars. He also contributed to Libby Titus's second self-titled album, producing "The Night You Took Me To Barbados In My Dreams" (co-written by Titus and Hirth Martinez) and producing and playing guitar on "Miss Otis Regrets." He co-produced "The Best of Everything," originally intended for the film The King of Comedy, which instead appeared on Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers' Southern Accents album; he also worked on the horn arrangements and brought in Band alumni Richard Manuel and Garth Hudson as guests. In 1986, he played guitar on the track "The Morning" for the album Reconciled by the Call. That same year, he was brought on as creative consultant for Hail! Hail! Rock 'n' Roll (1987), a film honoring Chuck Berry, appearing on camera interviewing Berry and playing guitar while Berry recited poetry. In 1988, he collaborated with Maria McKee on the song "Nobody's Child," released on her 1989 debut album. In 1992, he produced "Love in Time" for Roy Orbison's posthumous album King of Hearts, a basic demo Orbison had recorded and rediscovered, which Robertson enhanced with new arrangements to make it sound as if the arrangements were original. Robertson began work on his first solo album, Robbie Robertson, in July 1986 after signing with Geffen Records, choosing Daniel Lanois as producer. The album was recorded at The Village Recorder in West Los Angeles, Bearsville Studios near Woodstock, in Dublin with U2, and in Bath, England with Peter Gabriel; it featured guest appearances by U2, Gabriel, Bodeans, and Maria McKee, with Garth Hudson and Rick Danko also contributing. He wrote "Fallen Angel" in honor of Richard Manuel after his death in March 1986. Released on October 26, 1987, the album peaked at No. 35 on the Billboard 200, remaining in the top 40 for three weeks and reached No. 23 on the UK Albums Chart, staying on the chart for 14 weeks. It received critical acclaim and was listed among the top 10 albums of 1987 by Billboard and ranked No. 77 on Rolling Stone's 1989 list of the 100 Best Albums of the Eighties. His biggest UK hit was "Somewhere Down the Crazy River," which reached No. 15 and stayed in the chart for 11 weeks; its video was directed by Martin Scorsese and featured Maria McKee in an acting role. In the U.S., the album had several hits on the Billboard Mainstream Rock charts, with "Showdown At Big Sky" reaching #2 and "Sweet Fire Of Love" reaching #7. The album was nominated for a Grammy for "Best Rock / Vocal Album" and certified gold in the U.S. in 1991. In Canada, Robertson won Album of the Year, Best Male Vocalist of the Year, and Producer of the Year at the 1989 Juno Awards. In 1991, Rod Stewart recorded a version of "Broken Arrow" for his album Vagabond Heart, which reached No. 20 on the Billboard 100 and No. 2 on the Top Canadian Hit Singles chart; the song was also performed live by the Grateful Dead with Phil Lesh on vocals. Storyville was released on September 30, 1991; Robertson collaborated with New Orleans natives like Aaron and Ivan Neville and the Rebirth Brass Band, bringing in Garth Hudson and Rick Danko as contributors. The album reached No. 69 on the Billboard 200 and received positive reviews, with Rolling Stone giving it 4 1/2 stars and the Los Angeles Times 3 stars. Two tracks, "What About Now" and "Go Back To Your Woods," charted on the Mainstream Rock charts at No. 15 and No. 32 respectively. The album was nominated for Grammy Awards in "Best Rock Vocal Performance (solo)" and "Best Engineer." In 1994, Robertson formed the Red Road Ensemble and recorded Music for the Native Americans, which accompanied a TBS documentary series; the song "Ghost Dance" outlines the Battle of Wounded Knee and the near-extinction of the bison. On Contact from the Underworld of Redboy, he explored rock, native, and electronic music with Howie B, DJ Premier, and Marius de Vries (Björk, Massive Attack), examining native traditions like Peyote healing; Rolling Stone gave it 4 out of 5 stars, and he won a Juno Award for Best Music of Aboriginal Canada Recording. Released on April 5, 2011, How to Become Clairvoyant was his fifth solo release, stemming from impromptu demo sessions in Los Angeles with Eric Clapton; he performed "Straight Down The Line" with Robert Randolph and the Roots on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. The deluxe edition included five bonus tracks (four demos and "Houdini," named after Harry Houdini) and was released with a limited collector's edition featuring an art book, five lithographs (including by Richard Prince and Anton Corbijn), original tarot cards, original tracks, and ten bonuses. Released on September 20, 2019, Sinematic was his sixth solo album, featuring Van Morrison on "I Hear You Paint Houses" and allusions to Scorsese's films, with guest appearances by Citizen Cope, Derek Trucks, and Frédéric Yonnet. Robertson assisted Scorsese on the music for Raging Bull (1980), which sparked his interest in film music; he produced three newly recorded instrumental jazz tracks featuring guitar and performances by Garth Hudson and Richard Manuel, one co-written with Hudson, and selected the film's opening theme from Cavalleria Rusticana by Pietro Mascagni; the soundtrack was released in 2005 as a 37-track, 2-CD set. He worked with Scorsese on The King of Comedy (1983), credited for "Music Production," and contributed the original song "Between Trains" in tribute to assistant "Cowboy" Dan Johnson. In June 1986, he began work on The Color of Money, composing the score for the first time and bringing in Canadian jazz composer Gil Evans for orchestration; the best-known song, "It's in the Way That You Use It," co-written by Robertson and Eric Clapton, reached No. 1 on the Billboard Mainstream Rock Songs chart in January 1987; he also produced "Don't Tell Me Nothin'" with blues player Willie Dixon, co-written with Robertson. In 1999, he contributed songs to Oliver Stone's film Any Given Sunday. He scored Scorsese's 2019 film The Irishman and consulted with music supervisor Randall Poster on the soundtrack; the film is dedicated to him and he received a posthumous Academy Award nomination for Best Original Score, becoming the first Indigenous person nominated in that category. After The Last Waltz, MGM/UA viewed Robertson as a potential film actor and provided him with an office on the MGM lot; Martin Scorsese's agent contacted him about producing a film about traveling carnivals, which he found appealing due to his childhood carnival experiences. The screenplay was directed by Robert Kaylor. Although initially only intended as producer, Robertson became the third lead actor, playing Patch, with Gary Busey as Frankie and Jodie Foster as Donna; real-life carnies were cast alongside professional actors, creating a difficult on-set atmosphere. Carny opened on June 13, 1980, and Warner Bros. released a soundtrack co-credited to Robertson and Alex North, re-released on CD in 2015. In November 2024, Robertson posthumously appeared in the documentary Return of the King: The Fall and Rise of Elvis Presley. In October 2025, he posthumously appeared in the documentary series Mr. Scorsese. He co-authored Legends, Icons and Rebels: Music That Changed the World with his son Sebastian Robertson and colleagues Jim Guerinot and Jared Levine, and wrote Hiawatha and the Peacemaker, illustrated by David Shannon. His autobiography, Testimony, was published by Crown Archetype in November 2016. In April 2025, Penguin Random House Canada announced a second volume of his memoirs, focusing on his relationship with Martin Scorsese, to be published in November 2025. On March 24, 1968, Robertson married Dominique Bourgeois.

Robertson was ranked 59th in Rolling Stone magazine's 2011 list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time. The soundtrack for the film was re-released on compact disc by Real Gone Music in 2015. In November 2024, Robertson posthumously appeared in the documentary Return of the King: The Fall and Rise of Elvis Presley. In October 2025, he posthumously appeared in the documentary series Mr. Scorsese. Robertson co-authored Legends, Icons and Rebels: Music That Changed the World with his son, Sebastian Robertson, and colleagues Jim Guerinot and Jared Levine. He also wrote Hiawatha and the Peacemaker, illustrated by David Shannon. His autobiography, Testimony, written over the course of five years, was published by Crown Archetype in November 2016. In April 2025, Penguin Random House Canada announced that a second volume of Robertson's memoirs, focusing on his working relationship with Martin Scorsese, would be published in November 2025. On March 24, 1968, Robertson married Dominique Bourgeois, a Canadian journalist; they had two daughters and a son named Sebastian, and the marriage ended in divorce. On March 12, 2023, Robertson married his girlfriend of four years, Canadian entrepreneur, restaurateur, and Top Chef Canada judge Janet Zuccarini; their marriage occurred only five months before his death. Robertson was involved in social causes and was a member of the Canadian charity Artists Against Racism, using his platform to support anti-racism initiatives and public awareness campaigns. Robertson died at a Los Angeles hospital on August 9, 2023, at the age of 80, after a year-long battle with prostate cancer. His longtime manager, Jared Levine, stated that Robertson was surrounded by his family at the time of his death. In lieu of flowers, Levine requested that donations be made to the Six Nations of the Grand River, honoring Robertson’s heritage and lifelong connection to the community. In November 2023, director Martin Scorsese held a tribute concert for Robertson in Los Angeles, with notable guests including Joni Mitchell, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Lily Gladstone. In October 2024, another tribute concert with Scorsese's involvement was held at the Kia Forum. In May 2024, Robertson's three adult children filed a lawsuit against his wife, Janet Zuccarini, alleging elder abuse and undue influence, claiming that during a period of significant health decline, Zuccarini took advantage of Robertson's weakened condition to have him sign legal documents that would financially benefit her in the event of his death, without the full awareness or involvement of his children. The Band (including Robertson) was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 1989 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1994. In 1997, Robertson received a Lifetime Achievement Award from the National Academy of Songwriters. In 2003, Robertson received the Indspire Aboriginal Lifetime Achievement Award and was inducted into Canada's Walk of Fame. In 2005, Robertson received an honorary doctorate from York University. In 2006, he received the Governor General's Performing Arts Award for Lifetime Artistic Achievement, Canada's highest honour in the performing arts. In 2008, Robertson and the Band received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. In 2011, Robertson was inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame. On May 27, 2011, Robertson was made an Officer of the Order of Canada by Governor General David Johnston. In 2014, the Band was inducted into Canada's Walk of Fame. On October 14, 2017, Robertson received the first Lifetime Achievement Award from the community of Six Nations. In 2019, Robertson was given a key to the city of Toronto by Mayor John Tory during a TIFF press conference for Once Were Brothers: Robbie Robertson and The Band. In 2019, Robertson received the Lifetime Achievement Award in the Canadian Music Industry Hall of Fame from Canadian Music Week (CMW).
